summary: Instance-based xorshift32 PRNG: the same seed always replays the same sequence, independent of UnityEngine.Random.
problem: UnityEngine.Random is one global stream shared by every script in the project, which makes it useless for anything that must be reproducible. Seed it for your dungeon generator and the particle system, an animation event and a third-party asset all pull from the same stream in between, so the same seed produces a different dungeon on the next run — or on a different machine, or after you add one Random.value call somewhere unrelated. A SeededRandom is its own stream: nothing else can touch it, so a level seed, a replay, or a daily challenge shared between players regenerates identically every time. xorshift32 is chosen because it is four integer operations with a single uint of state — cheap enough to create thousands of them, and small enough to reason about.

workedExample.setup: Why the constructor hashes the seed instead of using it directly — traced through the raw xorshift first, then through the hash that now runs before it.
steps: WITHOUT hashing, state would start at 1. state ^= state << 13 gives 1 ^ 8192 = 8193.
state ^= state >> 17: 8193 >> 17 is 0, so state stays 8193.
state ^= state << 5: 8193 << 5 = 262176. The two values share no set bits, so the XOR is a plain sum: 8193 + 262176 = 270369.
Seeds 2 and 3 follow the identical no-overlap path and yield 540738 and 811107 — exactly 2x and 3x. The first draw was proportional to the seed.
WITH hashing, the seed is avalanched first: 1, then ^= >>16 leaves 1, then *0x7feb352d = 2146121005, then ^= >>15 = 2146159355, then *0x846ca68b = 1753872457, then ^= >>16 = 1753845952.
xorshift then runs on 1753845952 and returns 145099912; seed 2 gives 289945872 and seed 3 gives 3078990264.
workedExample.result: First NextFloat() for seeds 1, 2 and 3 is now 0.033784, 0.067508 and 0.716883 — unrelated values. Across 50,000 sequential one-shot seeds the mean is 0.4997 and all ten deciles land within 1.5 percent of even. Before the hash was added those same three seeds gave 0.000063, 0.000126 and 0.000189, so a one-shot new SeededRandom(levelIndex).NextFloat() was barely random at all.

useCases: Procedural level generation from a level seed, so the same seed always produces the same dungeon, cave or maze.
Daily-challenge or weekly-run seeds that must produce identical content for every player.
Replays and deterministic simulation, where random decisions have to be reproduced exactly on playback.
Deterministic decoration: give each chunk or room a SeededRandom keyed on its coordinates and it regenerates identically without storing anything.
Tests that need repeatable randomness without the global state of UnityEngine.Random leaking between cases.

usage.codeNote: Draw in a fixed order — the sequence is reproducible, but only if every run consumes values in the same order. An early-out or a conditional draw will desynchronise everything after it.

apiNotes.NextFloat(): Takes the top 24 bits of NextUInt() and scales by 2^-24, which caps the result at 16777215/16777216 = 0.99999994f. Genuinely [0, 1): the obvious NextUInt() / (float)uint.MaxValue reaches exactly 1f, and that is what this used to do. No precision is lost — a float never held more than 24 of the 32 bits.
apiNotes.NextFloat(float, float): min + NextFloat() * (max - min). Since NextFloat() is strictly below 1, max is never returned.
apiNotes.NextInt(int, int): min + NextUInt() % (max - min), with max EXCLUSIVE to match UnityEngine.Random.Range's int overload. The range is passed through Mathf.Max(1, ...), so it never throws.
apiNotes.NextBool(float): NextFloat() < chance, defaulting to a fair coin. NextBool(0f) is always false and NextBool(1f) is always true, both exactly, because the range of NextFloat() is closed at 0 and open at 1.
apiNotes.NextVector2(float, float): Two independent NextFloat(min, max) draws, so it consumes TWO values from the stream, not one. A rectangle sample, not a disc — it is not uniform over a circle.

gotchas.title: The seed is hashed, so a given seed no longer matches older builds
gotchas.body: The constructor avalanches the seed (the lowbias32 finalizer) before xorshift ever runs, which is what makes sequential seeds independent. It also means every seed now produces a DIFFERENT sequence than it did before this fix: a level, dungeon or daily challenge generated from a stored seed will not reproduce content generated by an older build. Seeds in save files still replay consistently from here on — they just describe different content than they used to.

gotchas.title: Reproducibility still depends on a fixed draw order
gotchas.body: Hashing fixes the quality of the stream, not the discipline of consuming it. The sequence replays identically only if every run draws the same values in the same order, so an early-out, a conditional draw, or a reordered loop desynchronises everything after it.

gotchas.title: NextInt never throws, even for invalid ranges
gotchas.body: Mathf.Max(1, max - min) means NextInt(5, 5) and NextInt(5, 0) both return 5 rather than erroring. A range bug therefore shows up as a suspiciously constant value rather than an exception. There is also the usual modulo bias when (max - min) does not divide 2^32 evenly, which is negligible for gameplay-sized ranges.

gotchas.title: The state cannot be read, saved or restored
gotchas.body: `state` is private with no accessor, so you cannot snapshot a generator mid-sequence into a save file. To resume, store the original seed plus how many values were consumed, and re-draw them on load — which also means your generation code has to consume a deterministic count.

gotchas.title: Not thread-safe
gotchas.body: NextUInt mutates a single uint field with no synchronisation. Two threads sharing one instance will interleave reads and writes and destroy reproducibility. Give each thread or job its own instance, seeded deterministically.

gotchas.title: Deliberately minimal API
gotchas.body: There is no NextVector3, no shuffle, no weighted pick and no Gaussian. ProbabilityUtils has those, but every one of them uses the global UnityEngine.Random and cannot be pointed at a SeededRandom — so a reproducible weighted pick has to be written by hand on top of NextFloat().
